desc:
Every node of a binary search tree is the root of a subtree. The median of a subtree with s values is its ((s + 1) / 2)-th smallest value, where the division rounds down (so for an even size the smaller of the two middle values is used).

Return the sum of the medians of the subtrees rooted at all nodes of the tree. Every node counts once, including leaves, whose median is their own value.

Sorting the values of every subtree separately is O(n² log n) on a path-shaped tree. Aim for O(n).

Tree encoding. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level order. The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn, level by level, from left to right. A missing child is written as -1 (node values are never negative, so -1 cannot be confused with a value). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped. The empty tree is [].

For example, [5,2,7,-1,3,6] is the tree whose root 5 has left child 2 and right child 7; node 2 has no left child and right child 3; node 7 has left child 6 and no right child.

Example 1

tree = [4,2,6,1,3,5,7]
Output: 28
Leaves 1, 3, 5, 7 give 16. Node 2 has {1,2,3} so 2, node 6 has {5,6,7} so 6, and the root has seven values with median 4. Total 16 + 2 + 6 + 4 = 28.

Example 2

tree = [1,-1,2,-1,3]
Output: 7
Subtree of 1 is {1,2,3} with median 2, subtree of 2 is {2,3} with median 2 (smaller middle value), subtree of 3 is {3}. Total 2 + 2 + 3 = 7.
constraints: 0 ≤ node value ≤ 100,000, all values distinct; the tree is a valid BST
The sum always fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: For a small tree you can collect the values of each subtree, sort them and pick the median. What property of a BST makes the sorting unnecessary?
Look at the inorder (ascending) sequence of the whole tree. Which part of it belongs to a given subtree?

Every subtree occupies a contiguous block of the global inorder sequence, starting at (rank of the node) - (size of its left subtree) and of length equal to its size. Read the median straight from that block.
editorial: In a BST the values of any subtree are consecutive in the inorder order of the whole tree. If a node has inorder position pos (0-based) and its left subtree has L nodes, then its subtree starts at pos - L and spans s positions. The median is therefore the element at index pos - L + (s - 1) // 2 of the inorder array.

So the algorithm computes the inorder array and each node's position once, computes the subtree sizes (children are processed before parents by iterating over the level-order numbering backwards), and adds one array lookup per node. The total is O(n) time and O(n) memory, with no sorting and no recursion.
